trt-acts-of-union.why: Scotland had been badly shaken by the collapse of the Darien scheme, its costly attempt to found a colony in Panama in the 1690s. The two parliaments then clashed over who would succeed Anne, and England's Alien Act of 1705 threatened Scottish trade unless Scotland negotiated a union.
trt-acts-of-union.impact: Scotland kept its own legal system, church and universities, while gaining free access to English markets and colonial trade. The union survived Jacobite risings in 1715 and 1745, and in 1801 a further union with Ireland created the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.

trt-first-geneva-convention.why: Dunant set out his ideas in A Memory of Solferino in 1862. A Geneva committee of five, which later became the International Committee of the Red Cross, took them up, and the Swiss government invited states to a diplomatic conference to turn the proposal into binding law.
trt-first-geneva-convention.impact: The convention was revised in 1906 and 1929, and after the Second World War four new Geneva Conventions of 1949 extended protection to prisoners and civilians. Every state in the world has since ratified them, and Dunant shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

trt-alaska-purchase.why: The Russian fur trade in Alaska was in decline, and officials feared Britain could seize the territory from neighbouring Canada in any future war. Secretary of State William Seward, eager to expand American influence in the Pacific, agreed a price of 7.2 million dollars.
trt-alaska-purchase.impact: Gold rushes from the 1890s, including the Klondike stampede through Alaskan ports and the strike at Nome, drew thousands north. Alaska became a territory in 1912 and a state in 1959, and the oil found at Prudhoe Bay in 1968 transformed its economy.

trt-japan-surrender.why: In August 1945 the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and the Soviet Union declared war and invaded Manchuria. Emperor Hirohito then broke a deadlock in his government and announced by radio on 15 August that Japan would accept the Allied terms.
trt-japan-surrender.impact: Allied forces under MacArthur occupied Japan until 1952. A new constitution in 1947 made the emperor a symbol, gave women the vote and renounced war, war crimes trials were held in Tokyo, and the San Francisco treaty of 1951 formally restored Japan's sovereignty.

trt-partial-test-ban.why: Hundreds of atmospheric tests had spread radioactive fallout worldwide, and scientists found strontium-90 building up in children's teeth. The United States, Britain and the Soviet Union could not agree on inspections to verify a full ban, so underground tests were left out of the deal.
trt-partial-test-ban.impact: France and China refused to sign and carried on testing in the atmosphere for years. The treaty opened the way to the Outer Space Treaty of 1967 and the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968, and a Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty was agreed in 1996.

trt-korean-armistice.why: By mid-1951 the front had settled into a costly stalemate near the 38th parallel. Talks dragged on mainly over prisoners of war, as many Chinese and North Korean captives refused to go home, until Stalin's death and pressure from the new Eisenhower government helped break the deadlock.
trt-korean-armistice.impact: A demilitarised zone about four kilometres wide was created along the ceasefire line. South Korea's president Syngman Rhee refused to sign, the United States agreed a defence treaty with Seoul and kept troops there, and the two Koreas developed in sharply different directions.

trt-warsaw-pact.why: Western powers had agreed to let West Germany rearm and join NATO, which alarmed Moscow after two world wars against Germany. The Soviet Union wanted a formal alliance that would justify keeping its troops in Eastern Europe and give it a counterweight to NATO in negotiations.
trt-warsaw-pact.impact: When Hungary tried to leave in 1956 Soviet forces crushed the uprising. Albania drifted away in the 1960s and formally withdrew in 1968, and Romania refused to join the invasion of Czechoslovakia. The pact was formally dissolved in July 1991, months before the Soviet Union collapsed.

trt-oslo-accords.why: The First Intifada, a Palestinian uprising from 1987, had shown that the occupation could not simply continue. The PLO was weakened after backing Iraq in the Gulf War, Rabin was elected in 1992 promising peace, and Norwegian researchers set up secret back-channel talks.
trt-oslo-accords.impact: Israel and the PLO recognised each other, and a Palestinian Authority was set up in Gaza and parts of the West Bank. A second agreement followed in 1995, but Rabin was assassinated that November, and the core issues of borders, Jerusalem and refugees were never settled.

trt-kyoto-protocol.why: The first report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in 1990 warned that human emissions were warming the planet. The UN climate convention signed at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit set only voluntary goals, and governments agreed in 1995 to negotiate binding targets.
trt-kyoto-protocol.impact: The protocol came into force in 2005 after Russia ratified it. It created carbon trading and offset schemes and encouraged the EU's own emissions trading system, but it set no limits for fast-growing developing economies such as China, and Canada withdrew in 2011.

trt-brexit.why: The 2016 referendum produced a 52 to 48 per cent vote to leave. Parliament rejected Theresa May's withdrawal deal three times, and she resigned. Boris Johnson renegotiated the arrangements for Northern Ireland and won a large majority in the December 2019 election, which let the agreement pass.
trt-brexit.impact: A Trade and Cooperation Agreement was signed on 24 December 2020, avoiding tariffs on goods but bringing new customs paperwork. Free movement of people between Britain and the EU ended, and checks on goods between Great Britain and Northern Ireland remained a long political dispute.

trd-coca-cola-first-sold.why: Pemberton had earlier sold French Wine Coca, a drink of wine and coca extract. When Atlanta voted to ban alcohol in 1886, he developed a sweet non-alcoholic syrup with coca and kola nut, mixed with carbonated water at Jacobs' Pharmacy. His bookkeeper Frank Robinson named it and wrote the flowing logo.
trd-coca-cola-first-sold.impact: Candler pushed the brand with coupons, signs and advertising, and bottling rights sold in 1899 made it available far beyond soda fountains. The cocaine was removed in the early 1900s, the contour bottle arrived in 1915, and Coca-Cola became a symbol of American culture worldwide.

trd-dow-jones-average.why: Charles Dow, Edward Jones and Charles Bergstresser founded Dow Jones and Company in 1882 to publish financial news, and launched the Wall Street Journal in 1889. Dow had already published an average made up mostly of railroad stocks, and wanted a simple gauge of the newer industrial firms.
trd-dow-jones-average.impact: The average became the best known measure of the American stock market. It peaked at 381 before the 1929 crash and sank to about 41 in 1932, first closed above 1,000 in 1972, and fell by almost 23 per cent on Black Monday in 1987.

trd-ford-assembly-line.why: Demand for the Model T, launched in 1908, far outstripped what Ford's Highland Park plant could build. His engineers borrowed ideas from flour mills, the overhead lines of Chicago meatpackers and interchangeable parts, and first tested a moving line on magnetos before applying it to the whole car.
trd-ford-assembly-line.impact: The repetitive work drove huge staff turnover, so in 1914 Ford doubled pay to five dollars a day. More than fifteen million Model Ts were eventually built, and moving-line mass production spread across manufacturing worldwide, a system that became known as Fordism.

trd-first-walmart.why: Walton ran franchised Ben Franklin variety stores in Arkansas, and when the franchise's executives turned down his idea of discount stores in small towns, he opened his own in Rogers, Arkansas. The same year Kmart, Target and Woolco also launched, as discount retailing took off across America.
trd-first-walmart.impact: Walmart went public in 1970 and built its own distribution centres and truck fleet, and was an early adopter of barcodes and satellite links between stores. Its low prices drew shoppers but were also blamed for closing small-town shops and for holding down wages.

trd-decimal-day.why: Britain had argued about decimal coinage for over a century, and the florin was introduced in 1849 as a tenth of a pound. After South Africa, Australia and New Zealand switched in the 1960s, a government committee recommended the change and the decision was announced in 1966.
trd-decimal-day.impact: The 50p coin had already replaced the ten-shilling note in 1969, and new halfpenny, penny and twopenny coins went into use. Shoppers complained that traders rounded prices up. The halfpenny was withdrawn in 1984, while the 20p and pound coins followed in the early 1980s.

trd-apple-founded.why: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak had met as young men in California, and Wozniak showed his home-built computer at the Homebrew Computer Club. When the Byte Shop ordered fifty machines, Jobs sold his Volkswagen van and Wozniak his HP calculator to pay for parts, and Ronald Wayne joined as a third founder.
trd-apple-founded.impact: The Apple II of 1977, with colour graphics and a case, was one of the first successful mass-produced personal computers. Apple floated on the stock market in 1980. Jobs was forced out in 1985 and returned in 1997, leading the company to the iPod and iPhone.

trd-amazon-founded.why: Jeff Bezos was working at a New York investment firm when he read that use of the web was growing by more than 2,000 per cent a year. He chose books because millions of titles could never fit in one shop, and set up near Seattle, close to tech talent and a major book distributor.
trd-amazon-founded.impact: Amazon floated in 1997 and spread from books to almost every kind of product, reshaping retail and publishing. It launched Prime in 2005, Amazon Web Services in 2006, which made renting cloud computing mainstream, and the Kindle e-reader in 2007.

trd-kroc-mcdonalds.why: In 1948 Dick and Mac McDonald had stripped their drive-in down to a short menu of burgers, fries and shakes, made on a kitchen run like a factory line. Kroc, a travelling salesman of Multimixer milkshake machines, opened his first franchise in Des Plaines, Illinois.
trd-kroc-mcdonalds.impact: Kroc bought out the brothers in 1961 for 2.7 million dollars, and the company made much of its money by owning the land under its restaurants. The Big Mac and Happy Meal followed, and McDonald's became a symbol of American influence as it spread to over a hundred countries.

trd-dot-com-peak.why: Netscape's soaring share launch in 1995 convinced investors that the web would make fortunes. Venture capital was easy to raise, online brokers let ordinary people trade shares from home, and many start-ups were valued on visitor numbers rather than profits, while the Federal Reserve was raising interest rates.
trd-dot-com-peak.impact: The Nasdaq hit 5,048 in March 2000 and sank to around 1,100 by October 2002, wiping out trillions of dollars. Survivors such as Amazon and eBay emerged stronger, the fibre-optic cable laid in the boom later carried broadband, and the index did not regain its peak until 2015.

trd-bitcoin-pizza.why: Bitcoin had been described in a 2008 paper by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto and launched in January 2009. It had no established price and almost nothing could be bought with it, so programmer Laszlo Hanyecz offered 10,000 bitcoin on a forum to show it could pay for real goods.
trd-bitcoin-pizza.impact: The trade is often cited as the first real-world purchase made with bitcoin. Exchanges soon began quoting prices, bitcoin passed one dollar in 2011, and when it climbed above 60,000 dollars in 2021 the two pizzas were worth hundreds of millions of dollars.

spt-pele-first-world-cup.why: Brazil had been haunted by losing the deciding match of the 1950 World Cup to Uruguay at the Maracana in Rio. For 1958 coach Vicente Feola built a gifted side around Didi, Garrincha and Vava, and brought along a 17-year-old from Santos who had already played for his country.
spt-pele-first-world-cup.impact: Pele became the youngest player to score in a World Cup final, and Brazil remain the only South American side to win the tournament in Europe. They retained the trophy in 1962 and won again in 1970, and Pele became the most famous footballer in the world.

spt-england-world-cup.why: England were awarded the tournament in 1960. Alf Ramsey, appointed manager in 1963, boldly predicted England would win and built a disciplined side that often played without wingers. Months before the finals the Jules Rimet trophy was stolen in London and found by a dog named Pickles.
spt-england-world-cup.impact: England beat West Germany 4-2 after extra time and Bobby Moore lifted the trophy at Wembley. Ramsey was knighted, and it remains England's only men's World Cup. The win set expectations that later teams struggled to meet, a weight later summed up in the song Three Lions.

spt-fight-of-the-century.why: Ali was stripped of his title in 1967 after refusing to be drafted for Vietnam, and Frazier won the championship during his exile. When Ali was allowed to box again in 1970 both men were unbeaten, and each was guaranteed 2.5 million dollars for the bout at Madison Square Garden.
spt-fight-of-the-century.impact: Months later the Supreme Court overturned Ali's draft conviction. He beat Frazier on points in a 1974 rematch, regained the title against George Foreman that year, and won their brutal third fight, the Thrilla in Manila, when Frazier's corner stopped it in 1975.

spt-first-cricket-world-cup.why: Limited-overs cricket had grown in England since the Gillette Cup began in 1963, and the first one-day international was played in Melbourne in 1971 after a Test was washed out. A women's World Cup in England in 1973 came first, and the men's event followed with eight teams.
spt-first-cricket-world-cup.impact: Clive Lloyd's century helped the West Indies beat Australia by 17 runs at Lord's. India's shock win over the West Indies in the 1983 final sparked a cricket boom across South Asia, and later tournaments brought coloured clothing, a white ball and floodlit matches.

spt-rugby-world-cup-mandela.why: International sporting boycotts against apartheid kept South Africa out of the first two Rugby World Cups in 1987 and 1991. After the country's first democratic election in 1994 it hosted the 1995 tournament, and Mandela backed the Springboks when many in the ANC wanted their emblem dropped.
spt-rugby-world-cup-mandela.impact: Mandela presented the trophy to captain Francois Pienaar wearing a Springbok shirt. Rugby union turned professional within weeks of the final, and South Africa went on to win again in 2007, 2019 and 2023, with Siya Kolisi becoming their first Black captain to lift the trophy.

spt-tiger-woods-masters.why: Coached from early childhood by his father Earl, Woods won three straight US Amateur titles from 1994 to 1996 before turning professional. Augusta National had no Black members until 1990, and Lee Elder had become the first Black golfer to play the Masters only in 1975.
spt-tiger-woods-masters.impact: At 21 Woods became the youngest Masters champion, and television audiences and prize money surged. Augusta was lengthened to counter big hitters, a response nicknamed Tiger-proofing. He held all four major titles at once in 2000 and 2001 and won his fifteenth major at the 2019 Masters.

spt-london-olympics-opening.why: London beat Paris to win the Games in July 2005, and the city was hit by suicide bombings the following day. The Olympic Park was built on former industrial land in Stratford, east London, and film director Danny Boyle was chosen to stage the opening ceremony, called Isles of Wonder.
spt-london-olympics-opening.impact: The Queen appeared in a film with Daniel Craig as James Bond before a stunt double parachuted into the stadium. Team GB won 29 gold medals, including three on the evening known as Super Saturday, and the Olympic Stadium later became West Ham United's home ground.

spt-leicester-champions.why: Leicester were bottom of the Premier League in April 2015 before winning seven of their last nine games to stay up. Claudio Ranieri replaced Nigel Pearson that summer, the club had signed N'Golo Kante, and bookmakers offered odds of 5,000 to 1 against them winning the title.
spt-leicester-champions.impact: Bookmakers paid out large sums, and Leicester reached the Champions League quarter-finals the next season. Ranieri was sacked in 2017 and stars such as Kante and Mahrez were sold. Owner Vichai Srivaddhanaprabha died in a helicopter crash at the stadium in 2018, and the club won the FA Cup in 2021.

spt-kipchoge-sub-two.why: In 2017 Nike staged a similar attempt on a motor racing circuit at Monza, where Kipchoge ran 2:00:25. He set an official world record of 2:01:39 in Berlin in 2018, and the INEOS 1:59 Challenge then chose a flat, tree-lined course in Vienna's Prater park for another try.
spt-kipchoge-sub-two.impact: Kipchoge ran 1:59:40. The prototype carbon-plated shoes worn by him and other runners fuelled a debate about technology, and World Athletics brought in rules on shoe design in 2020. The next day Brigid Kosgei broke the women's marathon world record in Chicago.

spt-messi-world-cup.why: Messi had lost the 2014 World Cup final to Germany in extra time and three Copa America finals, and briefly retired from international football in 2016. Argentina's Copa America win over Brazil in 2021 ended a long title drought, but they began the 2022 tournament by losing to Saudi Arabia.
spt-messi-world-cup.impact: Argentina won on penalties after a 3-3 draw, their third world title after 1978 and 1986. Messi won the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player and an eighth Ballon d'Or in 2023. Qatar 2022 was also the first World Cup held in the Middle East and in winter.

art-pride-and-prejudice.why: Austen drafted the novel in 1796 and 1797 under the title First Impressions. Her father offered it to a London publisher, who turned it down without reading it. After Sense and Sensibility sold well in 1811, she reworked the manuscript and it appeared anonymously as by the author of that book.
art-pride-and-prejudice.impact: Elizabeth Bennet and Mr Darcy became models for countless romantic leads. The novel has been adapted many times, notably in the 1995 BBC series with Colin Firth, and reimagined in books such as Bridget Jones's Diary. Austen appeared on the Bank of England ten-pound note from 2017.

art-frankenstein.why: The eruption of Tambora in 1815 caused the cold, stormy year without a summer in 1816, which kept the writers indoors at Byron's villa. Mary, then eighteen, had heard talk of galvanism, experiments using electricity to make dead muscles twitch, and imagined a scientist giving life to a creature.
art-frankenstein.impact: Stage versions were drawing crowds by 1823, and Mary revised the novel in 1831, adding an introduction on its origins. Boris Karloff's 1931 film created the flat-headed monster most people picture, and the name Frankenstein became shorthand for a creation that escapes its maker's control.

art-christmas-carol.why: In 1843 Dickens read a government report on child labour and visited a ragged school for poor children in London, and he resolved to strike a blow for the poor. His latest serial, Martin Chuzzlewit, was selling disappointingly and he needed money, so he turned to a short Christmas story.
art-christmas-carol.impact: The first 6,000 copies sold out by Christmas Eve, though the costly binding left Dickens little profit, and pirated versions soon appeared. He later gave public readings of it, and it has been adapted for stage and screen ever since, making Scrooge a byword for a miser.

art-statue-of-liberty.why: French jurist Edouard de Laboulaye proposed a monument to American independence and liberty after the Union victory in the Civil War. France paid for the statue and Americans were to fund the pedestal, but money ran short until Joseph Pulitzer's newspaper raised it from small donations.
art-statue-of-liberty.impact: The statue became the first sight of America for millions of immigrants arriving through nearby Ellis Island from 1892. A plaque with Emma Lazarus's poem The New Colossus was added in 1903, the copper weathered to green, and it was restored for its centenary in 1986.

art-mona-lisa-stolen.why: Leonardo's portrait had been in French royal hands since the reign of Francis I and hung in the Louvre, admired but not yet world famous. Security was lax, and Peruggia, who had helped fit glass cases in the museum, hid inside and walked out with the painting under his smock.
art-mona-lisa-stolen.impact: During the search the poet Guillaume Apollinaire was arrested and Pablo Picasso questioned. After Peruggia's arrest in Florence the painting was shown in Italy and returned to the Louvre in January 1914. Peruggia, who claimed he wanted it back in Italy, served only a few months in prison.

art-jazz-singer.why: Warner Bros. was a smaller studio looking for an edge over its rivals, and it developed Vitaphone with Western Electric. Its 1926 film Don Juan had a recorded score and sound effects but no speech, and The Jazz Singer, adapted from a Broadway play, added songs and a few spoken lines.
art-jazz-singer.impact: Jolson's line 'You ain't heard nothin' yet' became famous. Warner's first all-talking feature followed in 1928, studios rushed to build sound stages, and some silent stars' careers ended. Sound-on-film soon replaced discs, and the film's use of blackface is now widely criticised.

art-steamboat-willie.why: Earlier in 1928 Walt Disney lost the rights to his character Oswald the Lucky Rabbit to his distributor. With animator Ub Iwerks he created Mickey Mouse, but two silent Mickey shorts failed to find a distributor, so after The Jazz Singer's success Disney made the third with synchronised sound.
art-steamboat-willie.impact: Mickey became a star and Disney grew into a major studio, releasing Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs in 1937. American copyright extensions, including a 1998 law nicknamed the Mickey Mouse Protection Act, delayed the short's entry into the public domain until January 2024.

art-star-wars.why: George Lucas had wanted to remake the Flash Gordon serials but could not get the rights, so he wrote his own space adventure. After the success of American Graffiti, Fox backed the film, and Lucas set up Industrial Light and Magic to create special effects that did not yet exist.
art-star-wars.impact: Lucas had kept the merchandising and sequel rights, which made him wealthy as toys sold in their millions. The film won six competitive Oscars, sequels followed in 1980 and 1983, Industrial Light and Magic led the field in visual effects, and Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012.

art-mtv-launch.why: Cable television was spreading across America in the late 1970s, and a Warner and American Express venture saw a gap for a channel aimed at young viewers. Record companies supplied promotional clips for free, and the first video played was Video Killed the Radio Star by the Buggles.
art-mtv-launch.impact: MTV was criticised for playing few Black artists in its early years until Michael Jackson's Billie Jean broke through in 1983. It launched the Video Music Awards in 1984 and later shifted towards original programmes such as the reality series The Real World.

art-live-aid.why: In October 1984 BBC reports by Michael Buerk showed a devastating famine in Ethiopia. Bob Geldof and Midge Ure wrote Do They Know It's Christmas?, recorded by Band Aid that December, and its huge sales and the American single We Are the World led to the idea of a global concert.
art-live-aid.impact: Live Aid was watched by a vast global television audience and raised well over a hundred million pounds. Phil Collins played both venues by flying across the Atlantic on Concorde. Critics later argued some aid helped Ethiopia's government, and Geldof organised the Live 8 concerts in 2005.

phi-the-prince.why: Machiavelli had served the Florentine republic as a senior official and diplomat, watching rulers such as Cesare Borgia at work. When the Medici returned to power in 1512 he was dismissed, then imprisoned and tortured in 1513, and retired to his farm to write while Italy was fought over by France and Spain.
phi-the-prince.impact: The Prince was printed in 1532, five years after Machiavelli died. The Church placed it on its Index of Prohibited Books in 1559, and Frederick the Great later wrote a reply called Anti-Machiavel. Many now see it as an early work of political science that separates politics from morality.

phi-newton-principia.why: In 1684 Halley, Robert Hooke and Christopher Wren debated whether a force weakening with the square of distance would produce the elliptical orbits Kepler had described. Halley visited Newton in Cambridge, learned he had already worked it out, and urged him to publish a full account.
phi-newton-principia.impact: Newton's laws explained the tides, the paths of comets and the motions of the planets, and Halley used them to predict the return of the comet named after him. Newtonian mechanics stood unchallenged until Einstein's relativity in the early twentieth century, and still guides engineering today.

phi-candide.why: The Lisbon earthquake of 1755 killed tens of thousands of people, and the Seven Years' War began the following year. Voltaire was outraged by the optimism of thinkers following Leibniz, who held that this is the best of all possible worlds, and mocked them through the tutor Pangloss.
phi-candide.impact: Candide was condemned by authorities in Geneva and Paris and placed on the Church's Index, yet it ran through many editions in its first year. It became one of the most read works of the Enlightenment, and gave English the word Panglossian for blind optimism.

phi-common-sense.why: Paine arrived in Philadelphia from England in 1774 with a letter of introduction from Benjamin Franklin. Fighting broke out at Lexington and Concord in 1775 and the king declared the colonies in rebellion, yet many Americans still blamed his ministers and hoped for reconciliation with the crown.
phi-common-sense.impact: Paine's plain language reached ordinary readers in a way earlier pamphlets had not. His later essays, The American Crisis, opened with 'These are the times that try men's souls' and were read to Washington's troops, and in 1791 his Rights of Man defended the French Revolution.

phi-rights-of-man-declaration.why: After the storming of the Bastille in July 1789, the National Assembly abolished feudal privileges on the night of 4 August. Deputies wanted a statement of principles for the new constitution, and Lafayette drew on the American Declaration of Independence, consulting Thomas Jefferson, then the American minister in Paris.
phi-rights-of-man-declaration.impact: The declaration did not give women equal rights, prompting Olympe de Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman in 1791, and slavery continued in French colonies until 1794. It influenced liberal constitutions across Europe and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948.

phi-origin-of-species.why: On the voyage of HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836, Darwin studied fossils and the wildlife of the Galapagos. Reading Thomas Malthus on population in 1838 gave him the idea of natural selection, and papers by him and Wallace were read together at the Linnean Society in 1858.
phi-origin-of-species.impact: The book sparked fierce debate, including the 1860 Oxford clash between Thomas Huxley and Bishop Samuel Wilberforce. Darwin applied his theory to humans in The Descent of Man in 1871, and in the twentieth century natural selection was combined with genetics to form modern evolutionary biology.

phi-das-kapital.why: After the failed revolutions of 1848, the year he and Engels published The Communist Manifesto, Marx went into exile in London and lived for years in poverty. Engels supported him from the family cotton business in Manchester, and Marx set out to explain how industrial capitalism worked.
phi-das-kapital.impact: A Russian translation appeared in 1872, the first in another language. The book's theory of surplus value, that profit comes from unpaid labour, shaped socialist parties and trade unions, and inspired the Bolsheviks in 1917 and later communist governments in China and elsewhere.

phi-universal-declaration-human-rights.why: The UN Charter of 1945 committed members to promote human rights, after the Holocaust and other wartime atrocities. A Commission on Human Rights was formed in 1946, and drafters including John Humphrey, Rene Cassin, Peng Chun Chang and Charles Malik worked to agree principles across cultures.
phi-universal-declaration-human-rights.impact: Forty-eight states voted for it and eight abstained, including the Soviet bloc, South Africa and Saudi Arabia. It was not legally binding, but it inspired the European Convention on Human Rights in 1950 and two binding UN covenants in 1966, and many national constitutions.

phi-silent-spring.why: DDT had been used widely since the Second World War against malaria and lice, and in the 1950s aircraft sprayed it over American towns and farms to kill insect pests. Carson, a marine biologist and bestselling author, began her research after a friend reported birds dying after spraying in Massachusetts.
phi-silent-spring.impact: Carson testified before Congress in 1963 but died of cancer in 1964. The book helped launch the modern environmental movement, with the first Earth Day in 1970, and a 2001 treaty restricted DDT worldwide while still allowing its limited use against malaria.

phi-i-have-a-dream.why: Earlier in 1963 police in Birmingham, Alabama, had turned dogs and fire hoses on young protesters, and President Kennedy then proposed a civil rights bill. A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin organised the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, which drew around 250,000 people to the Lincoln Memorial.
phi-i-have-a-dream.impact: King won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964, and the Voting Rights Act followed in 1965. He was assassinated in Memphis in 1968. A federal holiday in his honour was first observed in 1986, and a memorial to him opened in Washington in 2011.

reg-hungarian-revolution.why: Khrushchev's secret speech denouncing Stalin in February 1956 raised hopes across the Eastern Bloc, and unrest in Poland that year won it more freedom. On 23 October students in Budapest marched with demands including Soviet withdrawal, crowds toppled a giant Stalin statue, and secret police fired on protesters.
reg-hungarian-revolution.impact: Moscow installed Janos Kadar as leader, and Nagy was executed in 1958 after a secret trial. Western powers, distracted by Suez, did not intervene. In June 1989 Nagy was reburied before vast crowds, and 23 October became a national holiday when Hungary was declared a republic that day.

reg-brexit-referendum.why: Euroscepticism had long divided the Conservative Party, and UKIP topped the 2014 European elections. David Cameron promised an in-out referendum in 2013 to settle the issue, and campaigners argued about sovereignty and immigration, which had risen sharply since the EU expanded eastwards in 2004.
reg-brexit-referendum.impact: Leave won by about 52 to 48 per cent, and Cameron resigned the next morning. The pound fell to its lowest level against the dollar in over thirty years, Scotland and Northern Ireland voted to remain, and the government triggered the formal two-year exit process in March 2017.

reg-korean-war-begins.why: Korea, a Japanese colony from 1910, was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945 between Soviet and American occupation zones. Rival governments under Kim Il Sung in the North and Syngman Rhee in the South both claimed the whole peninsula, and Kim invaded after winning Stalin's approval.
reg-korean-war-begins.impact: The war tripled American defence spending, strengthened NATO and led the United States to protect Taiwan. Procurement orders boosted Japan's recovering economy. Millions of Koreans died or were displaced, and the division of the peninsula hardened into one of the Cold War's lasting fault lines.

reg-shinkansen-opens.why: As Japan's economy boomed in the 1950s the old Tokaido line between Tokyo and Osaka was overloaded. Railway chief Shinji Sogo and engineer Hideo Shima pushed for a new standard-gauge line, part funded by a World Bank loan, and it opened days before the 1964 Tokyo Olympics.
reg-shinkansen-opens.impact: The network spread to Kyushu, northern Honshu and Hokkaido, with a strong safety record and early earthquake detection systems. It showed that fast rail could compete with air travel, and France's TGV, opened in 1981, followed. Construction debts also weighed on the national railway, which was privatised in 1987.

reg-nigeria-independence.why: Britain had joined its northern and southern protectorates into a single colony in 1914. Nationalist parties grew after the Second World War, led by figures such as Nnamdi Azikiwe and Obafemi Awolowo, and a series of constitutions moved the country towards self-government as a federation of regions.
reg-nigeria-independence.impact: Nigeria became a republic in 1963, but two military coups in 1966 led to the Biafran civil war from 1967 to 1970, in which many hundreds of thousands died, mostly from famine. Oil wealth grew in the 1970s, and military rule lasted until 1999.

reg-suez-nationalised.why: The canal, opened in 1869, was run by a company controlled by French and British shareholders, and British troops guarded it until 1956. Nasser, in power after the 1952 army coup, had bought weapons from the Soviet bloc, prompting the United States and Britain to cancel the Aswan loans.
reg-suez-nationalised.impact: Egypt sank ships to block the canal, which stayed closed until 1957. British Prime Minister Anthony Eden resigned in January 1957, the UN sent its first armed peacekeeping force, and Nasser emerged as a hero of Arab nationalism. The canal closed again from 1967 to 1975.

reg-golden-gate-bridge.why: Before the bridge, ferries were the only way across the Golden Gate strait between San Francisco and Marin County. Many engineers thought the strong currents and deep water made a bridge impossible, but voters approved a 35 million dollar bond in 1930, despite the Depression.
reg-golden-gate-bridge.impact: A safety net under the deck saved the lives of 19 workers, though 11 men died during construction. The bridge opened Marin County to suburban growth, remained the world's longest suspension span until 1964, and became one of the most photographed structures on earth.

reg-hurricane-katrina.why: Much of New Orleans lies below sea level in a bowl ringed by levees, and the loss of coastal wetlands had removed a natural buffer against storm surges. A mandatory evacuation was ordered only the day before landfall, and many poorer residents had no car to leave the city.
reg-hurricane-katrina.impact: About eighty per cent of New Orleans flooded, and many residents never returned. The head of FEMA resigned, the Army Corps of Engineers admitted design flaws and rebuilt the flood defences at a cost of billions, and Katrina became one of the costliest disasters in American history.

reg-christ-the-redeemer.why: A religious monument on Corcovado mountain was first proposed in the 1850s. The idea was revived in the 1920s by Catholics in Rio de Janeiro, who worried about the country's secular turn after church and state were separated in 1889, and the project was funded largely by donations.
reg-christ-the-redeemer.impact: The statue stands 30 metres tall on an 8-metre pedestal, with arms spreading 28 metres. It became the best known symbol of Rio and of Brazil, has been repaired after lightning strikes, and is lit up to mark national and global events.

reg-falklands-war.why: Argentina had claimed the islands, which it calls the Malvinas, since Britain took control in 1833, and negotiations had stalled. Facing economic crisis and protests at home, the military junta under General Galtieri hoped a quick victory would win popular support, and believed Britain would not fight.
reg-falklands-war.impact: Argentina returned to democracy in 1983 under Raul Alfonsin, while victory helped Thatcher win a landslide that year. The islanders received full British citizenship, Argentina still claims the islands, and in a 2013 referendum 99.8 per cent of voters chose to remain British.

reg-cyclone-tracy.why: Darwin was an isolated city of fewer than 50,000 people, and many of its houses were lightly built with roofs that were not securely fixed down. Tracy was a small, intense cyclone that turned towards the city on Christmas Eve, when many people were celebrating rather than preparing.
reg-cyclone-tracy.impact: Most of Darwin's homes were destroyed or badly damaged. Major General Alan Stretton led the emergency relief and a reconstruction commission oversaw the rebuilding. The disaster led to stronger cyclone building standards across northern Australia and better public warning systems.

reg-sydney-olympics.why: Sydney narrowly beat Beijing in the 1993 vote to host the Games, which Australia had last staged in Melbourne in 1956. The Olympic Park at Homebush Bay was built on former industrial land, including old brickworks and waste dumps, which was cleaned up as part of a pledge to hold a Green Games.
reg-sydney-olympics.impact: Cathy Freeman, an Aboriginal athlete, lit the cauldron and then won the 400 metres, a moment widely seen as a symbol of reconciliation. Australia finished fourth in the medal table, and triathlon and taekwondo made their debut as Olympic medal sports.
